"Leeds United F.C.") in the playoff semi-final, thus failing to gain promotion.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-7) Despite transfer speculation, Nugent spent the following season at Preston, scoring 15 goals in 43 appearances, and winning England recognition.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-:1-8) Preston finished seventh in 2006–07.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-9)
texts.6:
After both [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunderland_A.F.C. "Sunderland A.F.C.") and [Portsmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_F.C. "Portsmouth F.C.") had bids in the region of £6 million accepted for the player, Nugent was eventually unveiled as a [Pompey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_F.C. "Portsmouth F.C.") player at a press conference alongside John Utaka on 11 July 2007.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-10) However, rumours followed just weeks later that [Derby County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_County_F.C. "Derby County F.C.") were considering a bid for Nugent and that he would be leaving Portsmouth in the same transfer window he arrived in.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-:2-12) In a post-match press conference following a League Cup match early on in Nugent's Pompey career, in which he scored his first goal for the club, Portsmouth manager Harry Redknapp publicly stated Nugent would be free to leave the club if the right offer came in to help fund a move for more players.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-:2-12) However, Nugent stated he wanted to stay at Portsmouth.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-13)
A possible loan deal to [Ipswich Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ipswich_Town_F.C. "Ipswich Town F.C.") fell through in early March 2008 with Jim Magilton, the Ipswich manager, left questioning Nugent's fitness.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-14)
texts.7:
Nugent appeared frequently for Portsmouth in the FA Cup, scoring a goal in their third-round tie against Ipswich Town.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-:0-6) His role culminated in coming on for John Utaka in the 69th minute of the final against [Cardiff City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff_City_F.C. "Cardiff City F.C."), eventually winning the trophy.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-Portsmouth_1%E2%80%930_Cardiff-15)
The next season and after 18 months at the club, Nugent scored his first Premier League goal– against former manager Harry Redknapp at [Tottenham Hotspur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C. "Tottenham Hotspur F.C.") in a 1–1 draw on 18 January 2009.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-16) Two matches later he scored his second goal at [Fulham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulham_F.C. "Fulham F.C.") and followed this up with his first league goal at Fratton Park, scoring against Liverpool on 7 February 2009.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-18) However, these were to be Nugent's only top flight goals for Pompey.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-19)
On 5 August 2009, it was reported that Nugent had been involved in an alleged bust-up with teammate Marc Wilson during Portsmouth's pre-season trip to Portugal.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-20) Both players were sent home and subsequently fined two weeks' wages by the club.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-21)
texts.8:
On 1 September 2009, it was reported that Nugent was in talks with Burnley about a loan move._[citation needed_] Thirty minutes after the transfer window closed it was reported that Burnley had signed Nugent on a six-month-long loan deal with a view to a permanent move, subject to Premier League clearance.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-22) On 12 September, he made his debut for _the Clarets_ when he replaced Martin Paterson 70 minutes into the match against Liverpool at Anfield.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-23) After coming on as a second-half substitute for the Clarets on his home debut against Sunderland, Nugent scored two goals, helping Burnley to a 3–1 win.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-24) Nugent signed another loan agreement with Burnley on 1 February which would keep him at the club on loan until June.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-25)
After failing to renegotiate a permanent deal with Burnley or attract an alternative Premier League club, Nugent returned to newly relegated Portsmouth in the 2010–11 pre-season._[citation needed_] He was a regular starter as a left sided forward.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-26) After an initial goal drought that saw him fail to hit the net until his goal in a 6–1 defeat of [Leicester City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester_City_F.C. "Leicester City F.C.") on 24 September 2010 (his first for Pompey since February 2009), Nugent finished the season as Portsmouth's top goalscorer, scoring 14 goals in all competitions._[citation needed_]
Nugent (left) playing for [Leicester City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester_City_F.C. "Leicester City F.C.") in 2014
texts.9: On 5 July 2011, Nugent signed for Leicester City on a three-year deal after his contract with Portsmouth expired.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-27) He made his competitive debut in a 1–0 win over [Coventry City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_City_F.C. "Coventry City F.C.") on 6 August 2011,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-28) scoring his first goal for the club in a 2–1 defeat to [Bristol City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_City_F.C. "Bristol City F.C.") on 17 August.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-29) On 18 February 2012, Nugent scored the winning goal to knock Premier League team [Norwich City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_City_F.C. "Norwich City F.C.") out of the FA Cup at Carrow Road and put Leicester through to the quarter-finals._[citation needed_] Nugent finished the 2011–12 season as the club's top goalscorer with 16 goals in all competitions._[citation needed_]
texts.17:
## International career
On 28 March 2007, Nugent made his debut as a late substitute for England in a UEFA Euro 2008 qualifying match against Andorra in Barcelona.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-Andorra_0%E2%80%933_England-56) He marked the occasion by scoring the final goal in a 3–0 win in the 93rd minute, tapping in a goal-bound shot from Jermain Defoe as it was about to cross the line.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-Andorra_0%E2%80%933_England-56) Nugent, in his post-match press interview, expressed genuine satisfaction over having accomplished a "1 Goal/1 Cap" national team record._[citation needed_] Nugent never received another England cap, and his 11-minute national team career is the shortest of any player who has scored for England.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-57)
Nugent was the first Preston player to play for the national team since Tom Finney some 49 years previously, as well as the first England national team footballer from a club playing in the Football League since David James of West Ham in 2003.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-:0-6)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-58) He was also the first Football League outfield player since Michael Gray of Sunderland in 1999.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-:1-8)
Nugent is an [Everton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everton_F.C. "Everton F.C.") supporter.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-59)

A possible loan deal to [Ipswich Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ipswich_Town_F.C. "Ipswich Town F.C.") fell through in early March 2008 with Jim Magilton, the Ipswich manager, left questioning Nugent's fitness.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-14)

Nugent appeared frequently for Portsmouth in the FA Cup, scoring a goal in their third-round tie against Ipswich Town.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-:0-6) His role culminated in coming on for John Utaka in the 69th minute of the final against [Cardiff City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff_City_F.C. "Cardiff City F.C."), eventually winning the trophy.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-Portsmouth_1%E2%80%930_Cardiff-15)
The next season and after 18 months at the club, Nugent scored his first Premier League goal– against former manager Harry Redknapp at [Tottenham Hotspur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C. "Tottenham Hotspur F.C.") in a 1–1 draw on 18 January 2009.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-16) Two matches later he scored his second goal at [Fulham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulham_F.C. "Fulham F.C.") and followed this up with his first league goal at Fratton Park, scoring against Liverpool on 7 February 2009.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-18) However, these were to be Nugent's only top flight goals for Pompey.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-19)
On 5 August 2009, it was reported that Nugent had been involved in an alleged bust-up with teammate Marc Wilson during Portsmouth's pre-season trip to Portugal.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-20) Both players were sent home and subsequently fined two weeks' wages by the club.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-21)

On 1 September 2009, it was reported that Nugent was in talks with Burnley about a loan move._[citation needed_] Thirty minutes after the transfer window closed it was reported that Burnley had signed Nugent on a six-month-long loan deal with a view to a permanent move, subject to Premier League clearance.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-22) On 12 September, he made his debut for _the Clarets_ when he replaced Martin Paterson 70 minutes into the match against Liverpool at Anfield.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-23) After coming on as a second-half substitute for the Clarets on his home debut against Sunderland, Nugent scored two goals, helping Burnley to a 3–1 win.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-24) Nugent signed another loan agreement with Burnley on 1 February which would keep him at the club on loan until June.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-25)
After failing to renegotiate a permanent deal with Burnley or attract an alternative Premier League club, Nugent returned to newly relegated Portsmouth in the 2010–11 pre-season._[citation needed_] He was a regular starter as a left sided forward.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-26) After an initial goal drought that saw him fail to hit the net until his goal in a 6–1 defeat of [Leicester City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester_City_F.C. "Leicester City F.C.") on 24 September 2010 (his first for Pompey since February 2009), Nugent finished the season as Portsmouth's top goalscorer, scoring 14 goals in all competitions._[citation needed_]
Nugent (left) playing for [Leicester City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester_City_F.C. "Leicester City F.C.") in 2014

On 5 July 2011, Nugent signed for Leicester City on a three-year deal after his contract with Portsmouth expired.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-27) He made his competitive debut in a 1–0 win over [Coventry City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry_City_F.C. "Coventry City F.C.") on 6 August 2011,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-28) scoring his first goal for the club in a 2–1 defeat to [Bristol City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_City_F.C. "Bristol City F.C.") on 17 August.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-29) On 18 February 2012, Nugent scored the winning goal to knock Premier League team [Norwich City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_City_F.C. "Norwich City F.C.") out of the FA Cup at Carrow Road and put Leicester through to the quarter-finals._[citation needed_] Nugent finished the 2011–12 season as the club's top goalscorer with 16 goals in all competitions._[citation needed_]

## International career
On 28 March 2007, Nugent made his debut as a late substitute for England in a UEFA Euro 2008 qualifying match against Andorra in Barcelona.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-Andorra_0%E2%80%933_England-56) He marked the occasion by scoring the final goal in a 3–0 win in the 93rd minute, tapping in a goal-bound shot from Jermain Defoe as it was about to cross the line.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-Andorra_0%E2%80%933_England-56) Nugent, in his post-match press interview, expressed genuine satisfaction over having accomplished a "1 Goal/1 Cap" national team record._[citation needed_] Nugent never received another England cap, and his 11-minute national team career is the shortest of any player who has scored for England.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-57)
Nugent was the first Preston player to play for the national team since Tom Finney some 49 years previously, as well as the first England national team footballer from a club playing in the Football League since David James of West Ham in 2003.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-:0-6)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-58) He was also the first Football League outfield player since Michael Gray of Sunderland in 1999.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-:1-8)
Nugent is an [Everton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everton_F.C. "Everton F.C.") supporter.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent#cite_note-59)

# Patriots release Lee Johnson, sign David Nugent off Practice Squad
## Foxboro, Mass.-The New England Patriots announced that they have released veteran punter Lee Johnson today. Subsequently, the team signed defensive lineman David Nugent off their practice squad to remain at 53 players on the active roster.
Oct 15, 2001 at 10:15 AM
*     
*     
*   [](mailto:?subject=Patriots%20release%20Lee%20Johnson,%20sign%20David%20Nugent%20off%20Practice%20Squad&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.patriots.com%2Fnews%2Fpatriots-release-lee-johnson-sign-david-nugent-off-practice-squad-149536 "Send email")  
*   Copied!
Foxboro, Mass.-The New England Patriots announced that they have released veteran punter Lee Johnson today. Subsequently, the team signed defensive lineman David Nugent off their practice squad to remain at 53 players on the active roster.
Johnson, 39, was in his 17th NFL season, including his third with the Patriots. The 6-foot-2-inch, 202-pound punter was signed by the Patriots as a free agent on Feb. 18, 1999. He played in 37 games and totaled 203 punts for 8,578 yards (42.3 avg.) for the Patriots in just over two years. His 42.3-yard average per punt ranks fifth in franchise history. In 17 seasons, Johnson has accumulated 1,187 career punts for 50,473 yards. Both represent NFL career punting records. He had 305 punts downed inside the 20 and 137 career touchbacks. He also had a career long 76-yard punt in the season opener at Cincinnati (9/9/01).

# Patriots release Lee Johnson, sign David Nugent off Practice Squad
## Foxboro, Mass.-The New England Patriots announced that they have released veteran punter Lee Johnson today. Subsequently, the team signed defensive lineman David Nugent off their practice squad to remain at 53 players on the active roster.
Nugent, 23, was originally drafted by the Patriots in the sixth round (201st overall) of the 2000 NFL draft out of Purdue. The 6-foot-4-inch, 295-pound defensive end appeared in six games as a rookie and was credited with one defensive tackle. He was waived by the Patriots on Sept. 2, 2001, but was re-signed to the practice squad on Sept. 4.

**David Michael Nugent** (born October 27, 1977) is an American former professional football player who was a defensive lineman for the New England Patriots and Baltimore Ravens of the National Football League (NFL). He played college football for the Purdue Boilermakers.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Nugent attended Houston High School[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-2) and later Purdue University, where he played football as a defensive tackle.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-4)

## Professional career
[edit]
Nugent was selected in the sixth round of the 2000 NFL draft by the New England Patriots.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-6) In his rookie season he played in six games.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-auto-7) In his second season after playing a backup role at defensive end for seven games Nugent made his first career start for the Patriots against the Cleveland Browns on December 9, 2001.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-8) Nugent and the Patriots went on to win their first Super Bowl championship that season on February 3, 2002, in Super Bowl 36.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-9) Following his release from the Patriots due to an injury in training camp the Baltimore Ravens signed Nugent to their active roster on October 29, 2002.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-10) Nugent played in nine games with the Baltimore Ravens at defensive end.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-auto-7) On September 5, 2003, the Ravens released Nugent following training camp.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-11) In February 2004 Nugent was allocated by the Oakland Raiders to the Rhein Fire of NFL Europe where after recording six sacks he earned 1st Team All NFL Europe honors.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-12)

## Professional career
In 2024, Nugent appeared in the Apple TV+ documentary series The Dynasty: New England Patriots.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:2-13) His interviews focused on his time living with quarterback Tom Brady during both players' rookie years and the period surrounding the franchise’s first Super Bowl championship.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-14) The series also utilizes archival home video footage provided by Nugent from that time.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:3-15)
In 2024, Nugent appeared as a guest on NewsNation’s _On Balance with Leland Vittert_ on multiple occasions, where he discussed professional development through the lens of his experiences living with quarterback Tom Brady during their early NFL careers.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:0-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:1-17)

Nugent Named Ivy League Player of the Year
November 21, 2001  | Men's Soccer
Share:
By: Princeton Athletic Communications
**Nov. 21, 2001**
PRINCETON, N.J. - Senior Mike Nugent (West Windsor, N.J.) has been named the Ivy League Men's Soccer Player of the Year, and is one of eight Princeton players to earn All-Ivy recognition this season. Nugent is the first Princeton player in 11 years to be selected as the Player of the Year . Tiger head coach Jim Barlow '91 won the award in 1990.
Nugent helped lead Princeton to a share of the Ivy League title and an automatic berth into the NCAA tournament. A two-time Ivy Player of the Week, Nugent was the force behind the Princeton offense, finishing the regular season with 12 goals and six assists, including five goals and two assists in league play. Nugent, a first-team All-Ivy in 1999, was a unanimous first-team selection this season.

# Nugent Named Ivy League Player of the Year
## Related News
Joining Nugent as unanimous selections to the first-team are classmate Matt Behncke (Williamsburg, Va.) and junior goalkeeper Jason White (Maple Glen, Pa.). Behncke, a first-team All-Ivy selection for the second-straight season, registered three goals and two assists in league play, and six goals and five assists overall for a Princeton squad that led the league in goals (34) and assists (36). White, an honorable mention selection in 2000, allowed 13 goals in 1,706 minutes of play. His goals-against average (0.69) was the best in the Ivy League. White also posted an Ivy-best 10 shutouts in 17 games played. Sophomore defender Jeff Hare (Richmond, Va.) rounds out Princeton's representatives on the first team. He led a Tiger defense that allowed an average of 0.76 goal per game, the best mark in the Ancient Eight.
Senior Graeme Rein (Birmingham, Ala.) and junior Bob Nye (Downingtown, Pa.), both defesemen, earned second-team All-Ivy honors. Rein registered a goal and an assist for Princeton while playing all 17 games. Nye played in all 17 games and finished with one assist.
Senior Lucas Moskowitz (Storrs, Conn.) and freshman Ryan Rich (Yorktown, Va.) earned honorable mention honors for the Tigers. Moskowitz finished the regular season with three goals and two assists in 16 games, and was third on the team with 25 shots. Rich had an outstanding freshman year for the Orange and Black. He had a league-leading eight assists while playing in all 17 games. Rich finished the regular season with one goal and 10 points, fourth best on the team.

# Nugent Named Ivy League Player of the Year
## Related News
Princeton (10-2-5) earned a first round bye in the NCAA tournament and will meet the winner of the Boston College/Farleigh Dickinson matchup on Sunday, Nov. 25 at 1 p.m. on Lourie-Love Field. The first round meeting between the Eagles and the Knights will take place at 7 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 23 on Lourie-Love Field. Tickets are $8 for adults and $5 for student and seniors. Weekend passes are $14 for adults and $9 students and seniors.

# Patriots release Lee Johnson, sign David Nugent off Practice Squad
## Foxboro, Mass.-The New England Patriots announced that they have released veteran punter Lee Johnson today. Subsequently, the team signed defensive lineman David Nugent off their practice squad to remain at 53 players on the active roster.
Oct 15, 2001 at 10:15 AM
*     
*     
*   [](mailto:?subject=Patriots%20release%20Lee%20Johnson,%20sign%20David%20Nugent%20off%20Practice%20Squad&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.patriots.com%2Fnews%2Fpatriots-release-lee-johnson-sign-david-nugent-off-practice-squad-149536 "Send email")  
*   Copied!
Foxboro, Mass.-The New England Patriots announced that they have released veteran punter Lee Johnson today. Subsequently, the team signed defensive lineman David Nugent off their practice squad to remain at 53 players on the active roster.
Johnson, 39, was in his 17th NFL season, including his third with the Patriots. The 6-foot-2-inch, 202-pound punter was signed by the Patriots as a free agent on Feb. 18, 1999. He played in 37 games and totaled 203 punts for 8,578 yards (42.3 avg.) for the Patriots in just over two years. His 42.3-yard average per punt ranks fifth in franchise history. In 17 seasons, Johnson has accumulated 1,187 career punts for 50,473 yards. Both represent NFL career punting records. He had 305 punts downed inside the 20 and 137 career touchbacks. He also had a career long 76-yard punt in the season opener at Cincinnati (9/9/01).

## Foxboro, Mass.-The New England Patriots announced that they have released veteran punter Lee Johnson today. Subsequently, the team signed defensive lineman David Nugent off their practice squad to remain at 53 players on the active roster.
Nugent, 23, was originally drafted by the Patriots in the sixth round (201st overall) of the 2000 NFL draft out of Purdue. The 6-foot-4-inch, 295-pound defensive end appeared in six games as a rookie and was credited with one defensive tackle. He was waived by the Patriots on Sept. 2, 2001, but was re-signed to the practice squad on Sept. 4.

**David Michael Nugent** (born October 27, 1977) is an American former professional football player who was a defensive lineman for the New England Patriots and Baltimore Ravens of the National Football League (NFL). He played college football for the Purdue Boilermakers.
texts.1:
## Early life and education
[edit]
Nugent attended Houston High School[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-2) and later Purdue University, where he played football as a defensive tackle.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-4)
texts.2:
## Professional career
[edit]
Nugent was selected in the sixth round of the 2000 NFL draft by the New England Patriots.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-6) In his rookie season he played in six games.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-auto-7) In his second season after playing a backup role at defensive end for seven games Nugent made his first career start for the Patriots against the Cleveland Browns on December 9, 2001.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-8) Nugent and the Patriots went on to win their first Super Bowl championship that season on February 3, 2002, in Super Bowl 36.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-9) Following his release from the Patriots due to an injury in training camp the Baltimore Ravens signed Nugent to their active roster on October 29, 2002.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-10) Nugent played in nine games with the Baltimore Ravens at defensive end.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-auto-7) On September 5, 2003, the Ravens released Nugent following training camp.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-11) In February 2004 Nugent was allocated by the Oakland Raiders to the Rhein Fire of NFL Europe where after recording six sacks he earned 1st Team All NFL Europe honors.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-12)
texts.3:
## Professional career
In 2024, Nugent appeared in the Apple TV+ documentary series The Dynasty: New England Patriots.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:2-13) His interviews focused on his time living with quarterback Tom Brady during both players' rookie years and the period surrounding the franchise’s first Super Bowl championship.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-14) The series also utilizes archival home video footage provided by Nugent from that time.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:3-15)
In 2024, Nugent appeared as a guest on NewsNation’s _On Balance with Leland Vittert_ on multiple occasions, where he discussed professional development through the lens of his experiences living with quarterback Tom Brady during their early NFL careers.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:0-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:1-17)

November 21, 2001  | Men's Soccer
Share:
By: Princeton Athletic Communications
**Nov. 21, 2001**
PRINCETON, N.J. - Senior Mike Nugent (West Windsor, N.J.) has been named the Ivy League Men's Soccer Player of the Year, and is one of eight Princeton players to earn All-Ivy recognition this season. Nugent is the first Princeton player in 11 years to be selected as the Player of the Year . Tiger head coach Jim Barlow '91 won the award in 1990.
Nugent helped lead Princeton to a share of the Ivy League title and an automatic berth into the NCAA tournament. A two-time Ivy Player of the Week, Nugent was the force behind the Princeton offense, finishing the regular season with 12 goals and six assists, including five goals and two assists in league play. Nugent, a first-team All-Ivy in 1999, was a unanimous first-team selection this season.

# Nugent Named Ivy League Player of the Year
## Related News
Joining Nugent as unanimous selections to the first-team are classmate Matt Behncke (Williamsburg, Va.) and junior goalkeeper Jason White (Maple Glen, Pa.). Behncke, a first-team All-Ivy selection for the second-straight season, registered three goals and two assists in league play, and six goals and five assists overall for a Princeton squad that led the league in goals (34) and assists (36). White, an honorable mention selection in 2000, allowed 13 goals in 1,706 minutes of play. His goals-against average (0.69) was the best in the Ivy League. White also posted an Ivy-best 10 shutouts in 17 games played. Sophomore defender Jeff Hare (Richmond, Va.) rounds out Princeton's representatives on the first team. He led a Tiger defense that allowed an average of 0.76 goal per game, the best mark in the Ancient Eight.
Senior Graeme Rein (Birmingham, Ala.) and junior Bob Nye (Downingtown, Pa.), both defesemen, earned second-team All-Ivy honors. Rein registered a goal and an assist for Princeton while playing all 17 games. Nye played in all 17 games and finished with one assist.
Senior Lucas Moskowitz (Storrs, Conn.) and freshman Ryan Rich (Yorktown, Va.) earned honorable mention honors for the Tigers. Moskowitz finished the regular season with three goals and two assists in 16 games, and was third on the team with 25 shots. Rich had an outstanding freshman year for the Orange and Black. He had a league-leading eight assists while playing in all 17 games. Rich finished the regular season with one goal and 10 points, fourth best on the team.

**David Michael Nugent** (born October 27, 1977) is an American former professional football player who was a defensive lineman for the New England Patriots and Baltimore Ravens of the National Football League (NFL). He played college football for the Purdue Boilermakers.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Nugent attended Houston High School[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-2) and later Purdue University, where he played football as a defensive tackle.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-4)

## Professional career
[edit]
Nugent was selected in the sixth round of the 2000 NFL draft by the New England Patriots.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-6) In his rookie season he played in six games.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-auto-7) In his second season after playing a backup role at defensive end for seven games Nugent made his first career start for the Patriots against the Cleveland Browns on December 9, 2001.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-8) Nugent and the Patriots went on to win their first Super Bowl championship that season on February 3, 2002, in Super Bowl 36.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-9) Following his release from the Patriots due to an injury in training camp the Baltimore Ravens signed Nugent to their active roster on October 29, 2002.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-10) Nugent played in nine games with the Baltimore Ravens at defensive end.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-auto-7) On September 5, 2003, the Ravens released Nugent following training camp.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-11) In February 2004 Nugent was allocated by the Oakland Raiders to the Rhein Fire of NFL Europe where after recording six sacks he earned 1st Team All NFL Europe honors.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-12)

## Professional career
In 2024, Nugent appeared in the Apple TV+ documentary series The Dynasty: New England Patriots.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:2-13) His interviews focused on his time living with quarterback Tom Brady during both players' rookie years and the period surrounding the franchise’s first Super Bowl championship.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-14) The series also utilizes archival home video footage provided by Nugent from that time.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:3-15)
In 2024, Nugent appeared as a guest on NewsNation’s _On Balance with Leland Vittert_ on multiple occasions, where he discussed professional development through the lens of his experiences living with quarterback Tom Brady during their early NFL careers.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:0-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Nugent_(American_football)#cite_note-:1-17)

Spain, through its alliance with France and as part of the Anglo-French War (1778–1783) with Britain, played an important role in the independence of the United States. Spain declared war on Britain as an ally of France, itself an ally of the American colonies, so Spain and the United States were cobelligerents. Most notably, Spanish forces attacked British positions in the south and captured West Florida from Britain in the siege of Pensacola. This secured the southern route for supplies and closed off the possibility of any British offensive through the western frontier of the United States via the Mississippi River. Spain also provided money, supplies, and munitions to the American forces.

Beginning in 1776, it jointly funded Roderigue Hortalez and Company, a trading company that provided critical military supplies. Spain provided financing for the final siege of Yorktown in 1781 with a collection of gold and silver in Havana, then Spanish Cuba.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-Chavez2004-1) Spain was allied with France through the Bourbon Family Compact and the Revolution was an opportunity to confront their common enemy, Great Britain. As the newly appointed Chief Minister of King Charles III of Spain, the Count of Floridablanca wrote in March 1777, "the fate of the colonies interests us very much, and we shall do for them everything that circumstances permit".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-2)

## Aid to the United States: 1776–1778
[edit]
Luis de Unzaga was the first Spanish official to provide direct military aid to the Continental Army during the American Revolution.
Spanish Louisiana governor Luis de Unzaga was given clear directives from Madrid and Havana: he was to remain officially neutral while quietly favoring the American rebels. This explains why, in April 1776, he provided safe harbor in New Orleans to several rebel ships fleeing the Royal Navy—an action that risked provoking British military retaliation and potentially forcing Spain into an immediate war. The following month, he established a front company in New Orleans under the name Roderigue Hortalez et Cie, naming the playwright Pierre-Augustin de Beaumarchais as its director. Through this fictitious firm, Unzaga secretly funneled gunpowder, firearms, blankets, food, medicines, and other essential supplies to the colonial rebels, all without arousing British suspicions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-recoveredmemories-3)
In July 1776, France and Spain agreed to finance the initial large-scale joint arms shipment. American diplomat Arthur Lee informed Congress that Spain would extend a confidential line of credit worth four million _reales de vellón_—equivalent to roughly 500,000 Continental dollars (more than $17 million in 2024 dollars).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-4) This marked Spain's initial aid to the poorly equipped Continental Army, funding the acquisition of 216 cannons, 27 mortars, 238 gun carriages, 12,826 grenades, 51,134 rounds, 300,000 pounds of gunpowder, 30,000 muskets with bayonets, 4,000 tents and 30,000 full uniforms. With the aid of these timely Spanish provisions, General Horatio Gates triumphed over General John Burgoyne at Saratoga on 17 October 1777.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-recoveredmemories-3)

## Aid to the United States: 1776–1778
Portrait by Francisco Jover y Casanova of Aranda
The same year, in correspondence with Spain’s envoy in Paris, the Count of Aranda from Aragon, Benjamin Franklin expressed gratitude for Spain’s further loan of nearly 200,000 livres in cash, “along with naval provisions from its harbors.”[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-unveilingmemories-5)
Spanish aid was supplied to the new nation through four main routes: from French ports with the funding of Rodrigue Hortalez and Company, through the port of New Orleans and up the Mississippi River, from the warehouses in Havana, and from Bilbao, through the Gardoqui family trading company. Spain made loans to the United States to be used to furnish war supplies through the House of Gardoqui.
Smuggling from New Orleans began in 1776 when General Charles Lee sent two Continental Army (the army of the United States) officers to request supplies from the New Orleans Governor, Luis de Unzaga. Unzaga, concerned about overtly antagonizing the British before the Spanish were prepared for war, agreed to assist the rebels covertly. Unzaga authorized the shipment of desperately needed gunpowder in a transaction brokered by Oliver Pollock, a Patriot (Revolutionary) and financier.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-6) When Bernardo de Gálvez y Madrid, Count of Gálvez was appointed Governor of New Orleans in January 1777, he continued and expanded the supply operations.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-7)

# Why did the US let Spain take Florida after the Revolutionary War even though it was previously owned by the British?
After his victory in Pensacola he gained a lot of renown even back in Spain, there were plans to use the chance to push out the British from the Caribbean altogether, there was a plan for an invasion of Jamaica which France also actively supported. And in the hype of the moment he was the man for that invasion. So probably aiming more towards that end he invaded the Bermudas instead of Saint Augustine, which meant cutting off the British from the Caribbean and therefore isolating Jamaica and facilitating the plans in the island.
With his success in Bermudas he spent a long time gathering men from Cuba and Spain to invade Jamaica, agreeing that France would put half the men (while Spain put the other half), but ultimately the French forces never arrived, Gálvez found himself awaiting the invasion with everything ready and the French constantly postponing it due to issues elsewhere. In the end peace was signed before the attack.
Britain accepted the independence of the 13 colonies and agreed peace with all the involved, they accepted granting Spain all the gained territories during the war (including Menorca back in Spain) and Spain traded the Bermudas for the remaining of Florida, which Britain happily accepted as Florida was cut off without the 13 and Jamaica was more compromised without Bermudas. An invasion from Spain on eastern Florida from Cuba, western Florida and Bermudas was the easiest, and having the Bermudas (which are islands) facilitated a far-away defence with simple naval power.
Bernardo Gálvez statue in front of the Spanish Embassy in the United States
* * *
So yes, Florida was reconquered during that war, and Bernardo Gálvez went on to become governor of Cuba at a young age and ultimately the last “big" Viceroy of New Spain before Mexican independence, which was the peak of any colonial politician, becoming one of the 4 Viceroys of the empire.

Spain at points in the 16th Century (1500s) did essentially CLAIM all of North America, but in reality never controlled any of it north of Florida and New Spain (today's Mexico), and their grip on parts of those territories was often tenuous.
From the early 17th Century (1607 to be precise) there was a permanent British presence in North America, and as the British solidified their grip on what is now Canada, their total holdings rivaled those of Spain on the North American continent by 1750, and may have exceeded them (borders were a trifle indistinct back then).
Spain ceded a large portion of New Spain to Napoleonic France, which then promptly sold the territory to the young United States in 1803. Those in possession of more history knowledge than Quorabot will probably recall the Louisiana Purchase.

# Why did the US let Spain take Florida after the Revolutionary War even though it was previously owned by the British?
Spain's grip on its New World holdings grew increasingly tenuous during the early 19th Century, and in 1819 Spain concluded the Hays-Onis Treaty with the United States, essentially trading Florida to the United States in exchange for the US assuming Spanish debts to the miniscule number of Florida residents, and fixing a boundary between the United States’ Louisiana Territory and New Spain. The treaty took effect in 1821 only months before Mexico declared its independence from the Spanish Crown, followed in rapid order by nearly all of Spain's mainland possessions in the Americas.
In short, Florida became an unchallenged, and inseverable (never mind that lunacy in the 1860s) part of the United States in 1821, achieving statehood in 1845, by which point Spain had been nearly totally evicted from North America (retaining only islands in the Caribbean) for over a decade.

# Why did the US let Spain take Florida after the Revolutionary War even though it was previously owned by the British?
Spain's grip on its New World holdings grew increasingly tenuous during the early 19th Century, and in 1819 Spain concluded the Hays-Onis Treaty with the United States, essentially trading Florida to the United States in exchange for the US assuming Spanish debts to the miniscule number of Florida residents, and fixing a boundary between the United States’ Louisiana Territory and New Spain. The treaty took effect in 1821 only months before Mexico declared its independence from the Spanish Crown, followed in rapid order by nearly all of Spain's mainland possessions in the Americas.
In short, Florida became an unchallenged, and inseverable (never mind that lunacy in the 1860s) part of the United States in 1821, achieving statehood in 1845, by which point Spain had been nearly totally evicted from North America (retaining only islands in the Caribbean) for over a decade.

Spain, through its alliance with France and as part of the Anglo-French War (1778–1783) with Britain, played an important role in the independence of the United States. Spain declared war on Britain as an ally of France, itself an ally of the American colonies, so Spain and the United States were cobelligerents. Most notably, Spanish forces attacked British positions in the south and captured West Florida from Britain in the siege of Pensacola. This secured the southern route for supplies and closed off the possibility of any British offensive through the western frontier of the United States via the Mississippi River. Spain also provided money, supplies, and munitions to the American forces.

## Aid to the United States: 1776–1778
[edit]
Luis de Unzaga was the first Spanish official to provide direct military aid to the Continental Army during the American Revolution.
Spanish Louisiana governor Luis de Unzaga was given clear directives from Madrid and Havana: he was to remain officially neutral while quietly favoring the American rebels. This explains why, in April 1776, he provided safe harbor in New Orleans to several rebel ships fleeing the Royal Navy—an action that risked provoking British military retaliation and potentially forcing Spain into an immediate war. The following month, he established a front company in New Orleans under the name Roderigue Hortalez et Cie, naming the playwright Pierre-Augustin de Beaumarchais as its director. Through this fictitious firm, Unzaga secretly funneled gunpowder, firearms, blankets, food, medicines, and other essential supplies to the colonial rebels, all without arousing British suspicions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-recoveredmemories-3)
In July 1776, France and Spain agreed to finance the initial large-scale joint arms shipment. American diplomat Arthur Lee informed Congress that Spain would extend a confidential line of credit worth four million _reales de vellón_—equivalent to roughly 500,000 Continental dollars (more than $17 million in 2024 dollars).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-4) This marked Spain's initial aid to the poorly equipped Continental Army, funding the acquisition of 216 cannons, 27 mortars, 238 gun carriages, 12,826 grenades, 51,134 rounds, 300,000 pounds of gunpowder, 30,000 muskets with bayonets, 4,000 tents and 30,000 full uniforms. With the aid of these timely Spanish provisions, General Horatio Gates triumphed over General John Burgoyne at Saratoga on 17 October 1777.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-recoveredmemories-3)

## Aid to the United States: 1776–1778
Portrait by Francisco Jover y Casanova of Aranda
The same year, in correspondence with Spain’s envoy in Paris, the Count of Aranda from Aragon, Benjamin Franklin expressed gratitude for Spain’s further loan of nearly 200,000 livres in cash, “along with naval provisions from its harbors.”[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-unveilingmemories-5)
Spanish aid was supplied to the new nation through four main routes: from French ports with the funding of Rodrigue Hortalez and Company, through the port of New Orleans and up the Mississippi River, from the warehouses in Havana, and from Bilbao, through the Gardoqui family trading company. Spain made loans to the United States to be used to furnish war supplies through the House of Gardoqui.
Smuggling from New Orleans began in 1776 when General Charles Lee sent two Continental Army (the army of the United States) officers to request supplies from the New Orleans Governor, Luis de Unzaga. Unzaga, concerned about overtly antagonizing the British before the Spanish were prepared for war, agreed to assist the rebels covertly. Unzaga authorized the shipment of desperately needed gunpowder in a transaction brokered by Oliver Pollock, a Patriot (Revolutionary) and financier.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-6) When Bernardo de Gálvez y Madrid, Count of Gálvez was appointed Governor of New Orleans in January 1777, he continued and expanded the supply operations.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-7)

> The Royal Court, British Crown's seat, with capital in London and court at Saint James Palace
Well no, the whole Seven Years War was Britain fighting to the last punch to keep and enlarge North American holdings. Thus when the war was over Britain was in bad money condition, and with a bunch of demanding Natives in the Mid West. And they solved it the obvious way: taxing the colonials and abiding by the concessions to Natives.

The Americans were not happy with this, in raw terms they wanted to pay less taxes and to keep expanding westwards. In abstract terms this was built on Liberal Enlightened principles: no taxation without representation.
Anyways, the anger boiled up, and they sank a cargo of tea departing from Boston after the Tea Law was passed, enforcing mercantilist tariffs on tea. A total of 6,500,000 Spanish dollars were given to the rebels by Spain in cash before Saratoga. Furthermore, the Spanish allowed American trade to dock both in New Orleans and Havana, something that was banned for the British (including Americans before becoming rebellious). Just this allowed them to keep fighting at all, a logistics story repeating itself later in the Civil War.

Spain declared war on Britain as an ally of France, itself an ally of the American colonies, so Spain and the United States were cobelligerents. Most notably, Spanish forces attacked British positions in the south and captured West Florida from Britain in the siege of Pensacola. This secured the southern route for supplies and closed off the possibility of any British offensive through the western frontier of the United States via the Mississippi River. Spain also provided money, supplies, and munitions to the American forces.

Beginning in 1776, it jointly funded Roderigue Hortalez and Company, a trading company that provided critical military supplies. Spain provided financing for the final siege of Yorktown in 1781 with a collection of gold and silver in Havana, then Spanish Cuba.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-Chavez2004-1) Spain was allied with France through the Bourbon Family Compact and the Revolution was an opportunity to confront their common enemy, Great Britain. As the newly appointed Chief Minister of King Charles III of Spain, the Count of Floridablanca wrote in March 1777, "the fate of the colonies interests us very much, and we shall do for them everything that circumstances permit".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-2)

## Aid to the United States: 1776–1778
[edit]
Luis de Unzaga was the first Spanish official to provide direct military aid to the Continental Army during the American Revolution.
Spanish Louisiana governor Luis de Unzaga was given clear directives from Madrid and Havana: he was to remain officially neutral while quietly favoring the American rebels. This explains why, in April 1776, he provided safe harbor in New Orleans to several rebel ships fleeing the Royal Navy—an action that risked provoking British military retaliation and potentially forcing Spain into an immediate war. The following month, he established a front company in New Orleans under the name Roderigue Hortalez et Cie, naming the playwright Pierre-Augustin de Beaumarchais as its director. Through this fictitious firm, Unzaga secretly funneled gunpowder, firearms, blankets, food, medicines, and other essential supplies to the colonial rebels, all without arousing British suspicions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-recoveredmemories-3)
In July 1776, France and Spain agreed to finance the initial large-scale joint arms shipment. American diplomat Arthur Lee informed Congress that Spain would extend a confidential line of credit worth four million _reales de vellón_—equivalent to roughly 500,000 Continental dollars (more than $17 million in 2024 dollars).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-4) This marked Spain's initial aid to the poorly equipped Continental Army, funding the acquisition of 216 cannons, 27 mortars, 238 gun carriages, 12,826 grenades, 51,134 rounds, 300,000 pounds of gunpowder, 30,000 muskets with bayonets, 4,000 tents and 30,000 full uniforms. With the aid of these timely Spanish provisions, General Horatio Gates triumphed over General John Burgoyne at Saratoga on 17 October 1777.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-recoveredmemories-3)

## Aid to the United States: 1776–1778
Portrait by Francisco Jover y Casanova of Aranda
The same year, in correspondence with Spain’s envoy in Paris, the Count of Aranda from Aragon, Benjamin Franklin expressed gratitude for Spain’s further loan of nearly 200,000 livres in cash, “along with naval provisions from its harbors.”[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-unveilingmemories-5)
Spanish aid was supplied to the new nation through four main routes: from French ports with the funding of Rodrigue Hortalez and Company, through the port of New Orleans and up the Mississippi River, from the warehouses in Havana, and from Bilbao, through the Gardoqui family trading company. Spain made loans to the United States to be used to furnish war supplies through the House of Gardoqui.
Smuggling from New Orleans began in 1776 when General Charles Lee sent two Continental Army (the army of the United States) officers to request supplies from the New Orleans Governor, Luis de Unzaga. Unzaga, concerned about overtly antagonizing the British before the Spanish were prepared for war, agreed to assist the rebels covertly. Unzaga authorized the shipment of desperately needed gunpowder in a transaction brokered by Oliver Pollock, a Patriot (Revolutionary) and financier.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-6) When Bernardo de Gálvez y Madrid, Count of Gálvez was appointed Governor of New Orleans in January 1777, he continued and expanded the supply operations.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_and_the_American_Revolutionary_War#cite_note-7)
